foodDescription: In Granada a small plate of food still comes free with every drink, and each round brings a different one. A few rounds make a dinner.
Young broad beans fried with cured ham and onion. A Granada classic, at its best in spring.
An omelet made with lamb brains and other offal, named after the cave quarter. Said to have been invented by monks at the Sacromonte Abbey.
A winter salad of orange, salt cod, black olives, onion, and olive oil, sometimes with hard-boiled egg. A Moorish-style mix of sweet and salty.
A mountain plate from the Alpujarra: fried potatoes and peppers, fried eggs, cured ham, chorizo, and blood sausage. Not a light lunch.
Cured ham from Trevélez, one of the highest villages in Spain, where cold, dry mountain air has cured hams for centuries.
Thin slices of fried eggplant drizzled with dark sugarcane molasses. A common tapa across eastern Andalusia.
Small rolls of sponge cake soaked in syrup and topped with toasted cream, from the town of Santa Fe, west of Granada. Named after Pope Pius IX.
Fried dough for dipping in thick hot chocolate. A breakfast, or the end of a long night out.
Sweet mint tea served in the teterías, small Moroccan-style tea houses that line the streets below the Albaicín, such as Calle Calderería Nueva.
The local beer, brewed in Granada since 1925. The free tapa usually arrives with a caña, a small glass of it.
A rough, homemade-style rosé or red from the Alpujarra villages, poured from the barrel in country bars.
